nodes.title: Cloud governance: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Governance is the set of policies and guardrails that keep a cloud account safe and on-budget as it scales from one engineer to a hundred. Think tagging standards, budget alerts, organizational policies, and the multi-account strategy.

flashcards.front: Why use multiple accounts (an Organization) instead of one big account?
flashcards.back: Blast-radius isolation: a compromised prod account doesn't leak into dev. Billing clarity: per-team or per-environment cost reports. Quota independence: prod doesn't share API limits with sandbox. Service Control Policies (AWS) / management groups (Azure) enforce 'no one can disable CloudTrail' across the whole org.

flashcards.front: What is a Service Control Policy (SCP)?
flashcards.back: An AWS Organizations policy that sets the maximum permissions any IAM identity in a member account can have. Even if a user's IAM policy grants `s3:*`, an SCP denying `s3:DeleteBucket` overrides it. SCPs are guardrails, not grants — they only restrict.

flashcards.front: Tagging strategy — name three high-leverage tags.
flashcards.back: (1) Owner / team — who pays and who to page. (2) Environment (prod/staging/dev) — drives access controls and lifecycle. (3) Cost-center / project — for chargeback. Tags are free and infinitely valuable for cost allocation and automation; enforce them with policies.

A pre-baked multi-account setup with security baselines: org with master + audit + log-archive + workload accounts, CloudTrail / Config enabled everywhere, SSO wired up, network templates ready. AWS Control Tower / Azure Landing Zones / GCP setup automate this so you start on a safe foundation, not bare cloud.

questions.q: A newly hired information security manager finds that the organization has no documented security strategy. Which action should be performed FIRST before drafting one?
choices: Understand the business strategy, objectives and risk appetite
Benchmark the security budget against industry peers
Select a control framework such as ISO 27001 or NIST CSF
Procure a governance, risk and compliance (GRC) platform
questions.explanation: CISM stresses that the security strategy must be derived from, and aligned with, the business strategy and the board-approved risk appetite. Without that context, any framework choice, budget benchmark or tool purchase is premature and risks producing a strategy disconnected from business value.

questions.q: The board asks the information security manager how to demonstrate that the security program is delivering value. Which metric BEST supports that conversation?
choices: Number of vulnerabilities patched per month
Percentage of staff completing the annual awareness module
Reduction in residual risk against the documented risk appetite
Count of firewall rule changes processed by the change board
questions.explanation: Boards think in terms of risk versus appetite, not operational tallies. Showing that residual risk is trending toward — and staying within — the approved risk appetite is the CISM-aligned way to evidence value delivery. Patch counts, training completion and rule-change volume are activity metrics, not outcome metrics.

questions.q: Which of the following is the MOST important reason for an organization to define a formal information security policy approved by senior management?
choices: It satisfies external auditors during certification audits
It documents the specific configuration baselines for systems
It allows the security team to discipline non-compliant employees
It establishes management intent and authority for the security program
questions.explanation: Policy, in CISM terms, is the formal expression of senior management's intent and the authority that underpins every standard, procedure and control below it. Audits, baselines and disciplinary action are downstream consequences — without leadership-endorsed intent, none of them carry weight.

questions.q: An organization documents that all laptops MUST use full-disk encryption with AES-256, and separately documents the click-by-click steps to enable it. In governance terms, what are these two documents respectively?
choices: A standard and a procedure
A policy and a guideline
A baseline and a policy
A guideline and a standard
questions.explanation: A standard specifies mandatory technologies or parameters that implement policy intent (AES-256 full-disk encryption); a procedure gives the step-by-step instructions for carrying it out. A policy is the high-level statement of management intent ('protect data on mobile devices'); guidelines are discretionary recommendations. CISM expects you to place each document in the policy → standard → procedure hierarchy.

questions.q: What is the PRIMARY function of an information security steering committee?
choices: To perform hands-on review and tuning of security tooling configurations across business units
To align the security program with business objectives and arbitrate priorities across stakeholders
To take over incident command from the security manager whenever a severity-one event occurs
To approve every firewall rule change so that network modifications receive executive oversight
questions.explanation: The steering committee brings business and IT leadership together to set direction, align security investment with business strategy, and resolve competing priorities — a governance function. It does not do technical work, command incidents, or approve operational changes; those belong to the security team, the incident response structure and change management respectively.

nodes.title: Incident Management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Incident Management. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: When establishing an incident response capability, which document defines the management-approved categorisation, escalation thresholds and communication ownership for security incidents?
flashcards.back: The incident response plan (IRP) is the management-endorsed document that codifies how incidents are classified, who is notified at each severity, who speaks to whom, and how decisions are made under pressure. The DR runbook deals with restoration of services, the AUP with end-user behaviour, and the MSA with vendor contractual terms — none of which replace the IRP.

flashcards.front: A ransomware incident is in progress. Threat actors have encrypted file servers and demand payment. As the information security manager directing the response, what should you do FIRST?
flashcards.back: CISM's incident-management domain is unambiguous: the first action is to activate the documented IRP and bring the response team together so that containment, communications, evidence preservation and recovery decisions are made under governance — not improvised. Negotiation, restore actions and media statements all happen later and only with the right authorities involved.

flashcards.front: After containing a major incident, the security manager is preparing the post-incident review. Which outcome BEST demonstrates that the review delivered value to the organization?
flashcards.back: The CISM-recommended outcome of a post-incident review is continuous improvement: weaknesses surfaced during the incident must feed back into the control environment, response runbooks and awareness programme so the same failure is harder to repeat. Blame, narrative polish and recognition are not the purpose of the review.

flashcards.front: An information security manager learns that a developer has stored production database credentials in a public source-code repository. What should be done FIRST?
flashcards.back: When credentials are confirmed exposed, the immediate priority is containment: rotate the secret and revoke any sessions or tokens it has produced, before anything else. Disciplinary action, repository migration and filter changes are appropriate follow-ups but do nothing to stop ongoing misuse of the leaked credential.

questions.q: When establishing an incident response capability, which document defines the management-approved categorisation, escalation thresholds and communication ownership for security incidents?
choices: The incident response plan
The disaster recovery runbook
The acceptable use policy
The vendor master service agreement
questions.explanation: The incident response plan (IRP) is the management-endorsed document that codifies how incidents are classified, who is notified at each severity, who speaks to whom, and how decisions are made under pressure. The DR runbook deals with restoration of services, the AUP with end-user behaviour, and the MSA with vendor contractual terms — none of which replace the IRP.

questions.q: A ransomware incident is in progress. Threat actors have encrypted file servers and demand payment. As the information security manager directing the response, what should you do FIRST?
choices: Negotiate the ransom amount with the threat actor
Restore from the most recent backups to minimise downtime
Activate the incident response plan and convene the response team
Notify the media to control the public narrative
questions.explanation: CISM's incident-management domain is unambiguous: the first action is to activate the documented IRP and bring the response team together so that containment, communications, evidence preservation and recovery decisions are made under governance — not improvised. Negotiation, restore actions and media statements all happen later and only with the right authorities involved.

questions.q: After containing a major incident, the security manager is preparing the post-incident review. Which outcome BEST demonstrates that the review delivered value to the organization?
choices: The report assigns individual blame for the breach
Senior management is given a polished narrative to share publicly
The investigation team receives recognition awards
Lessons learned are translated into updated controls, runbooks and training
questions.explanation: The CISM-recommended outcome of a post-incident review is continuous improvement: weaknesses surfaced during the incident must feed back into the control environment, response runbooks and awareness programme so the same failure is harder to repeat. Blame, narrative polish and recognition are not the purpose of the review.

questions.q: An information security manager learns that a developer has stored production database credentials in a public source-code repository. What should be done FIRST?
choices: Discipline the developer through HR for policy violation
Rotate the exposed credentials and revoke any active sessions tied to them
Open a change request to migrate the repository to a private host
Add the repository URL to the web filter denylist
questions.explanation: When credentials are confirmed exposed, the immediate priority is containment: rotate the secret and revoke any sessions or tokens it has produced, before anything else. Disciplinary action, repository migration and filter changes are appropriate follow-ups but do nothing to stop ongoing misuse of the leaked credential.

questions.q: A fire has made the primary data centre unusable and the recovery time objective for core services will clearly be exceeded. Who should formally declare a disaster and activate the business continuity plan?
choices: The first responder on site, because waiting for management approval wastes recovery time
Any member of the incident response team once two severity criteria have been met
The external emergency services commander, as the authority controlling the physical site
The individual or role designated with declaration authority in the BCP
questions.explanation: Disaster declaration triggers expensive, disruptive actions — failover, alternate-site activation, external communications — so the BCP must pre-designate who holds that authority (and successors), and that designated role makes the call. Site responders and emergency services control safety, not business recovery; leaving declaration to 'any team member' produces premature or conflicting activations.

nodes.title: Risk Management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Quick primer on Risk Management. Tap to flip cards covering the most-asked exam ideas in this domain.

flashcards.front: During a risk assessment a critical legacy application is found to have an unacceptable level of risk, and remediation will take 18 months. What should the information security manager recommend in the meantime?
flashcards.back: When risk exceeds appetite and remediation is not immediate, the CISM-recommended path is to layer compensating controls to reduce exposure and have the business owner — not the security manager — formally accept the residual risk for the interim period. Silent acceptance, paper-only transfer or unilateral decommissioning all bypass governance.

flashcards.front: Which of the following BEST describes the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
flashcards.back: ISACA defines inherent risk as the risk level in the absence of any controls, and residual risk as the level remaining after the current control environment is taken into account. The qualitative/quantitative split, asset/process split and ownership split are all distractors that ISACA explicitly rejects.

flashcards.front: A business unit proposes adopting a SaaS application that processes regulated customer data. From a CISM perspective, what is the MOST important step before approval?
flashcards.back: Third-party / supply-chain risk is now a major focus area on the CISM exam. Before onboarding a SaaS that touches regulated data, the security manager must assess the vendor's control environment and ensure the contract codifies the required obligations (breach notification, data location, audit rights, sub-processors). Uptime claims, firewall parity and ad-hoc penetration tests do not address the underlying governance question.

flashcards.front: The security manager tracks 'percentage of critical systems with patches older than 30 days' and alerts leadership when it crosses a threshold. What is this metric an example of?
flashcards.back: KRIs are forward-looking measures chosen to signal that risk is increasing before an incident materialises — exactly what a rising unpatched-systems percentage does. KGIs report whether goals were achieved after the fact; ROSI is a cost-benefit calculation; an SLA is a commitment between parties, not a measurement. Knowing KRI vs KPI vs KGI is core Domain 2 material.

questions.q: During a risk assessment a critical legacy application is found to have an unacceptable level of risk, and remediation will take 18 months. What should the information security manager recommend in the meantime?
choices: Accept the risk because remediation is already planned
Transfer the risk to the application owner with a signed memo
Implement compensating controls and obtain a formal risk acceptance
Decommission the application immediately to eliminate the exposure
questions.explanation: When risk exceeds appetite and remediation is not immediate, the CISM-recommended path is to layer compensating controls to reduce exposure and have the business owner — not the security manager — formally accept the residual risk for the interim period. Silent acceptance, paper-only transfer or unilateral decommissioning all bypass governance.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
choices: Inherent risk is qualitative; residual risk is quantitative
Inherent risk applies to assets; residual risk applies to processes
Inherent risk is owned by the security team; residual risk is owned by the business
Inherent risk is the exposure before controls; residual risk is what remains after controls are applied
questions.explanation: ISACA defines inherent risk as the risk level in the absence of any controls, and residual risk as the level remaining after the current control environment is taken into account. The qualitative/quantitative split, asset/process split and ownership split are all distractors that ISACA explicitly rejects.

questions.q: A business unit proposes adopting a SaaS application that processes regulated customer data. From a CISM perspective, what is the MOST important step before approval?
choices: Verify the vendor's marketing claims about uptime
Conduct a third-party risk assessment and review contractual security obligations
Confirm the SaaS provider uses the same firewall vendor as the organization
Require the business unit to fund a penetration test of the SaaS tenant
questions.explanation: Third-party / supply-chain risk is now a major focus area on the CISM exam. Before onboarding a SaaS that touches regulated data, the security manager must assess the vendor's control environment and ensure the contract codifies the required obligations (breach notification, data location, audit rights, sub-processors). Uptime claims, firewall parity and ad-hoc penetration tests do not address the underlying governance question.

questions.q: The security manager tracks 'percentage of critical systems with patches older than 30 days' and alerts leadership when it crosses a threshold. What is this metric an example of?
choices: A key goal indicator (KGI) confirming strategic objectives have been achieved
A return-on-security-investment (ROSI) calculation for the patching program
A key risk indicator (KRI) providing early warning that risk exposure is rising
A service level agreement (SLA) between the security team and system owners
questions.explanation: KRIs are forward-looking measures chosen to signal that risk is increasing before an incident materialises — exactly what a rising unpatched-systems percentage does. KGIs report whether goals were achieved after the fact; ROSI is a cost-benefit calculation; an SLA is a commitment between parties, not a measurement. Knowing KRI vs KPI vs KGI is core Domain 2 material.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: An information security manager is building the security program roadmap. Which input should have the GREATEST influence on prioritization of initiatives?
choices: The results of the latest business impact analysis and risk assessment
The penetration testers' most recent finding list
The CISO's personal experience at previous employers
The marketing roadmap published by the EDR vendor
questions.explanation: Program prioritization in CISM is risk-driven, not finding-driven, personality-driven or vendor-driven. The BIA tells you which assets and processes matter most to the business, and the risk assessment tells you where the unacceptable exposures are — together they drive where investment goes first.

questions.q: Which of the following is the PRIMARY purpose of separating duties between developers and production deployment staff?
choices: To comply with software licensing requirements
To reduce opportunities for unauthorized or unintentional changes to production
To allow the security team to bill change activity to development cost centers
To shorten the software release cycle
questions.explanation: Segregation of duties is a foundational preventive control: by ensuring that the person who writes code is not the person who deploys it to production, the organization reduces both fraud opportunity and the chance of an uncontrolled change reaching live systems. Licensing, cost allocation and release speed are unrelated to the control's intent.

questions.q: Who is PRIMARILY responsible for assigning the classification level of a customer database?
choices: The database administrator who manages and backs up the platform on a daily basis
The information owner in the business unit accountable for the data
The information security manager, since classification is a security activity
The internal audit function, which independently reviews data handling controls
questions.explanation: Classification is an accountability of the information owner — the business role that understands the data's value, sensitivity and regulatory obligations. The DBA is a custodian who implements the protections the classification requires; the security manager defines the classification scheme and advises; audit verifies compliance but owns nothing. Owner-vs-custodian distinctions are a recurring CISM theme.

questions.q: A critical application cannot be patched against a known vulnerability for six months due to vendor constraints. The security manager places the application behind a web application firewall with rules targeting the exploit and increases monitoring. What type of control has been applied?
choices: A corrective control, because it repairs the vulnerability in the application code
A deterrent control, because attackers will choose easier targets elsewhere
A directive control, because it instructs administrators how to operate the system
A compensating control, because it reduces the risk while the primary control is unavailable
questions.explanation: A compensating control is an alternative measure that provides comparable risk reduction when the primary control (patching) cannot be implemented. The WAF doesn't fix the code (not corrective), doesn't operate through discouragement (not deterrent), and isn't an instruction (not directive). CISM scenarios frequently test recognising compensating controls in patching-constraint situations.

questions.q: During business continuity planning, which exercise PRIMARILY determines the maximum tolerable downtime and acceptable data loss for each business process?
choices: Business impact analysis (BIA)
Penetration testing of the recovery site infrastructure
Tabletop walkthrough of the disaster recovery plan
Gap assessment against the chosen security framework
questions.explanation: The BIA quantifies the impact of disruption over time for each process and from that derives recovery objectives — RTO (maximum tolerable downtime) and RPO (acceptable data loss). Tabletop exercises validate plans that already exist; penetration tests assess technical security; framework gap assessments measure control coverage, not business criticality.

questions.q: At which point in a system development project is it MOST cost-effective for the security manager to ensure security is addressed?
choices: During user acceptance testing, when the system is functionally complete and realistic to assess
After go-live, when real traffic reveals which threats actually materialise in production
During requirements definition, so security needs shape the design from the start
During code review, when implementation flaws can be found line by line before release
questions.explanation: Security requirements defined at the start cost the least to implement — retrofitting controls after design, build or release multiplies the cost and often leaves architectural weaknesses unfixable. Testing, code review and production monitoring remain necessary layers, but the exam's 'MOST cost-effective' framing points at the earliest lifecycle involvement.

questions.q: Which measure BEST demonstrates that a security awareness program is actually changing employee behavior?
choices: A declining click rate across successive simulated phishing campaigns
The percentage of employees who completed the annual training module
The number of awareness posters and intranet articles published per quarter
Positive feedback scores collected at the end of each training session
questions.explanation: Behavioral metrics measure what people do, not what they attended: a falling click rate over repeated phishing simulations shows employees applying the training. Completion rates, content volume and satisfaction scores measure activity and sentiment — necessary for program management but not evidence of changed behavior. CISM consistently prefers outcome metrics over activity metrics.

questions.q: When reporting the state of information risk to the board of directors, which approach is MOST appropriate?
choices: Provide the full vulnerability scan output so the board can draw independent technical conclusions
Summarize top risks in business-impact terms with trends against the board-approved risk appetite
Limit the report to incidents that resulted in confirmed regulatory penalties during the period
Present the complete risk register with every entry's likelihood and impact scoring history
questions.explanation: Boards govern: they need a concise view of the most significant risks expressed in business terms (financial, operational, reputational), how exposure is trending, and where it stands relative to the appetite they approved. Raw scan output and full registers bury the signal; reporting only penalised incidents hides the forward-looking exposure the board is accountable for overseeing.
